summary: Sky Atlas is a web tool built for public view of the images from the SPHEREx mission, It blinks multiple images of the specified coordinates/celestial object that is provided which can help in observing how they change over time.
details:
Our project is a way of accessing data on Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, M31 (Andromeda), and the variable stars RW Aurigae and R Draconis. It renders data from FITS files on IRSA as images, making it easily accessible to everyone as a public tool.

By making the data public and convenient to explore, we can have many people analyzing it. If one person misses something, another person may be able to identify it. The impact of our project is that astronomical data becomes more accessible and easier for everyone to use.

We used AntiGravity, mostly Claude models and a few other models, for efficiency. The languages used were Java, CSS, and Python. Our hardware was a laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 5 processor and 8 GB of DDR5 RAM.

We used a variety of software and services, including Claude, AntiGravity, VS Code, GitHub, IRSA, Gaia, MAST, and Figma, and integrated them into our project. Our project focused on brainstorming ideas to decide what we should create.

How it works:
Our project uses a fast HTML, CSS, and JavaScript frontend connected to a Python FastAPI backend. Users can search for astronomical objects, such as Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, M31 (Andromeda), RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

The FastAPI backend uses Astroquery and Astropy to search the IRSA archive and retrieve available observation data. It then processes FITS files, which are a standard file format for astronomical images, and renders them as viewable images in the web application.

If the main IRSA data source is unavailable, the system falls back to the AWS DR1 source so that users can still access SPHEREx data. This makes the project more reliable and helps ensure that users can continue exploring observations even if one archive service has an outage.(which it is)

The API also includes integration with Gaia, which can provide information about nearby stars, including position, brightness, distance, and motion. Gaia was unavailable for part of our testing period, so we have not yet fully tested this feature. Once available, the Gaia integration can add useful context to the SPHEREx images and help users study the objects in greater detail.

By combining archive searches, FITS-image rendering, a fallback data source, and planned Gaia information, the project turns complex astronomical data into a tool that is easier for the public to explore and analyze.
